Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Appalachian Voices, Conservation Law

Foundation, Environmental Defense Fund, North Carolina Justice Center, Public Citizen, South

Carolina Coastal Conservation League, and Southern Alliance for Clean Energy (collectively,

Public Interest Organizations), protest the Application for Authorization under Section 203 of the

Federal Power Act and Requests for Confidential Treatment and Limited Waivers of Certain

Filing Requirements, filed by NextEra Energy, Inc. (NextEra) and Dominion Energy, Inc.

(Dominion) (together, Applicants), on July 15, 2026, in the above-captioned proceeding

(Application).2

            By virtue of its size, scale, and the diversity of business interests across both Applicants’

corporate structures, the Transaction presents novel threats to the public interest that do not fit

neatly within the Commission’s traditional merger-review framework. In order to assess the

Transaction’s consistency with the public interest, as required by the section 203 of the Federal

Power Act,11 and to protect the many ratepayers it will assuredly affect, the Commission must

apply a tailored review that accounts for the Transaction’s unique characteristics. The

Commission’s ability to conduct this review depends upon the Applicants to supply the necessary

information; section 203 places the burden of proving the Transaction’s harmony with the public

interest on the Applicants,12 and only upon such affirmative showing may the Commission

approve it.13 But the Applicants have not carried their burden here. By hewing strictly to the

path that previous, much smaller transactions, involving far fewer affected customers, have

taken, the Applicants fail to account for the unique implications the Transaction presents.

Further, they have sought waiver of many of the Commission’s required disclosures without

sufficient justification, further obscuring the Commission’s view into the Transaction’s potential

effects.

           In reviewing the Application, the Commission must account for the context in which the

Transaction would occur. As the Commission has recently recognized, “electricity demand in the

United States is expected to grow at an extraordinary pace in the near term, largely due to the

rapid growth of large loads.”14 Much of this expected load growth is concentrated in locations

affected by the Transaction, particularly Virginia and the Carolinas, where data center

       Yet the Transaction would enable the resulting entity to corner competitive generation

and transmission markets, all while expanding its pool of captive ratepayers on whom it can push

costs unimpeded. The size, buying power, and information access of the colossal combined

company would create clear competitive advantages that operate to the detriment of ratepayers

across the affected regions. It would have unmatched resources to build bespoke generation for

data centers across the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) footprint, aided by recent FERC and

PJM actions to encourage such arrangements. It would consolidate ownership of the only

nuclear units in ISO New England (ISO-NE) at a time when clean firm power comes at a

premium. It would also have the means and opportunity to dominate the growing share of

competitive, data center-related regional transmission projects in PJM, while maintaining a safe

pipeline of non-competitive Supplemental projects in the Dominion transmission zone (DOM

Zone). And each of these competitive activities could be insured on the backs of the largest

captive retail customer base in the world.

       Outside the affected Regional Transmission Organizations (RTO), the Transaction would

solidify and entrench the lack of meaningful competition among generation owners in the

Southeast. NextEra’s track record of suppressing competition in vertically integrated utility

areas threatens to halt even the minor moves toward expanded competition the region has taken

in recent years. Given the region’s disproportionate share of projected data center growth, any

ratepayers.

           And yet, these clear sources of harm to competition and ratepayer interests could very

well slip through the cracks of the Commission’s traditional merger review policies, as first

articulated in the Merger Policy Statement. 15 Such procedures were developed in a different era,

at the dawn of open access and generation competition.16 Despite significant upheaval in the

energy industry and changes in law since that time, the Commission’s approach has barely

changed. Its focus remains on the Appendix A Competitive Analysis Screen (Competitive

Analysis Screen) and Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI) values deemed acceptable three

decades ago. Consequently, this screen polices only a subset of transactions with significant

geographical overlap—reflecting the legal landscape and predominant merger types of the era—

and overlooks transactions like the one at issue in this case. The Commission’s traditional

review also ignores alternative theories of competitive harm where acceptable HHI thresholds

are satisfied, effectively foreclosing review of such geographically diverse transactions despite

the Competitive Analysis Screen’s structural indifference to them. Reliance on this sole

consideration of the Merger Policy Statement’s Effect on Competition prong also operates to the

exclusion of the other elements, which have become largely obsolete. Both the Effect on Rates

and Effect on Regulation inquiries have become box-checking exercises that do not attempt to

meaningfully assess a proposed transaction’s impacts so long as Applicants make the

conventional commitments. Likewise, the statutorily-required assessment of the potential for

cross-subsidization relies almost entirely on applicant representations rather than any searching

review.

          The Application adopts this playbook. The majority of its transmittal previews the

Delivered Price Test (DPT) results contained in Exhibit J.17 The Application touts up front and

throughout that the Transaction would result in minimal geographic overlap, 18 expecting that fact

to satisfy the Commission’s competition concerns. Its discussion of the Transaction’s effects on

rates19 and regulation20 are perfunctory and formulaic, reflecting the Commission’s relative lack

of concern with these issues in prior merger reviews. And the Application’s cross-subsidization

section blithely denies the potential for such intra-corporate dealings by repeating the

Commission’s four-part test without further elaboration. 21 Aside from one non-specific reference

to “longer term . . . customer benefits,”22 the Application makes no attempt to explain the

benefits the Transaction would create for the broader public. Rather, the Application treats

consistency with the public interest as coextensive with falling into an HHI safe harbor. The

result is an Application devoid of meaningful substance and incapable of supporting an informed

finding that the Transaction is consistent with the public interest.

         The Federal Power Act demands more. Far from eliminating competitive concerns, the

Transaction’s geographical reach creates unique threats of harm to competition, rates, and

regulation, as well as an enhanced likelihood of improper cross-subsidization. Reflexive retreat

to the Competitive Analysis Screen will overlook these harms. Instead, to ensure consistency

with the public interest and protect affected customers up and down the Eastern Seaboard, the

Commission must apply a more holistic review to the Transaction. Accordingly, Public Interest

Organizations respectfully request that the Commission reject the Application as incomplete
